strengths: Introduces a novel, extensible synthetic dataset of approximately 20,000 chaotic ODEs generated via an evolutionary algorithm with mutation, skew-product recombination, and chaos-selection tests; this is a substantive contribution for pretraining in nonlinear dynamics.

Proposes Panda, a dynamics-informed transformer architecture that combines patching, channel attention, Takens/delay-inspired augmentations, and polynomial/Fourier dynamics embeddings, with ablations isolating several architectural choices.

Provides broad zero-shot evaluation: 9.3k held-out synthetic systems, three experimental datasets, and two chaotic PDE benchmarks, showing consistent advantages over strong time series foundation model baselines such as Chronos, Chronos-SFT, TimesFM, and Time-MOE.

Demonstrates an interesting neural scaling law with respect to the number of unique training dynamical systems while holding total timepoints constant, which is a useful empirical finding for data diversity in SciML.

Includes exploratory analyses of attention maps, including nonlinear resonance-like structure and temporal-attention patterns, which, while preliminary, may motivate future work on interpretability of dynamics models.
weaknesses: The main zero-shot synthetic evaluation is still in-distribution with respect to the generative process: held-out systems are produced by the same mutation/skew-product pipeline from held-out founders, so the evaluation may overstate out-of-domain generalization relative to truly independent dynamical systems.

The comparison set is limited to time series foundation models and a fine-tuned Chronos variant. There is no comparison to specialized nonlinear-dynamics forecasting methods such as reservoir computing, next-generation reservoir computing, neural ODEs, DMD/Koopman methods, or PDE-specific SciML baselines, making the empirical case less convincing for a top-tier AI venue.

The PDE generalization claim rests on only two PDE examples (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and von Karman vortex street), without specialized PDE baselines or an ablation isolating which architectural components enable PDE transfer. The preprocessing/channelization of PDE fields is also insufficiently specified.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'universal representation,' 'emergent properties,' and patching being grounded in Takens' theorem. Patching contiguous time windows is not the same as a Takens delay embedding, and the resonance/attention analysis is suggestive rather than conclusive.

Ablation results are somewhat ambiguous: masked-language-model pretraining and the dynamics embedding interact in opposite ways across forecasting horizons, and it is not fully clear which components are used in the final model or why the final configuration is optimal.

Reproducibility is limited: the paper does not state whether the discovered dataset, code, or pretrained models are released, and details of baseline training, data splits, and evaluation procedures are partially relegated to appendices with some missing specifics.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: zero-shot forecasting of chaotic dynamical systems.
The evolutionary data generation pipeline for discovering synthetic chaotic ODEs is creative and potentially useful, with a large 20k-system dataset.
The architecture connects several dynamical-systems-inspired ideas: patching/Takens, channel attention for coupling, and random polynomial/Fourier features for dynamics embeddings.
The paper reports some promising empirical signals on held-out synthetic systems, real-world datasets, and PDE benchmarks, plus exploratory attention analysis.
The paper is generally well-structured and the motivation from nonlinear dynamics is clear.
weaknesses: The central claims of emergent universal representation and zero-shot PDE forecasting are overstrong relative to the evidence. The held-out synthetic test systems are generated by the same evolutionary/skew-product process as training, so they do not establish broad out-of-domain generalization.

The temporal attention description is concerning: using non-causal self-attention with NoPE (no positional encoding) would make patch representations permutation-invariant over time, removing the temporal order needed for forecasting. The manuscript does not justify or ablate this, undermining the architecture's plausibility.

Channel attention is used without positional/channel embeddings, yet the paper claims zero-shot PDE forecasting where spatial ordering and local coupling are essential. A permutation-invariant channel mixer cannot distinguish neighboring grid points/modes, so the PDE claim needs much stronger justification and controls.

Baselines and evaluation are insufficient/possibly unfair. Chronos-SFT is fine-tuned on 'our entire chaotic systems dataset' while Panda is zero-shot; if any held-out systems were included, the comparison is invalid. Standard dynamical-systems baselines (reservoir computing, neural ODEs, DMD/Koopman, LSTM/TCN, etc.) are missing.

The main metric, sMAPE, is known to saturate and can be misleading for chaotic time series; many other metrics are relegated to the appendix. Statistical significance and uncertainty quantification are limited.

Ablations are mixed: MLM pretraining and the dynamics embedding interact negatively in some settings, yet the paper concludes PolyEmbed is best. The paper does not isolate the contribution of NoPE, channel positional encoding, or the evolutionary data generation.

The scaling-law result is based on only eight synthetic dataset subsets and a fitted power law, without theory or validation across architectures/datasets; calling it a neural scaling law for differential equations is overstated.
Interpretability claims about nonlinear resonance and recurrence maps are qualitative and speculative, with no causal link to forecasting performance or downstream utility.

Real-world validation is narrow: only three low-dimensional selected experimental datasets, mostly compared against one baseline. Absolute errors, preprocessing, and hyperparameter tuning are not sufficiently transparent.
Reproducibility is weak: no code/data/model release is mentioned, the dataset-generation and chaoticity-filtering details are incomplete, and key implementation details are deferred or ambiguous.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale synthetic dataset of 20,000 chaotic ODEs via evolutionary recombination, addressing data scarcity for dynamics foundation models.

Combines dynamics-informed design (Takens-inspired patching, Koopman-inspired random polynomial/Fourier embeddings, channel attention) with a transformer, and ablations support the architectural choices.
Demonstrates strong zero-shot forecasting on held-out chaotic systems, experimental time series, and two PDE benchmarks, plus a neural scaling law showing the value of dynamical diversity.
Provides interpretability analyses (attention maps, nonlinear resonance patterns) that connect model behavior to dynamical systems concepts.
Paper is generally clear and includes extensive appendix details on data generation, training, and additional metrics.
weaknesses: The main zero-shot benchmark consists of held-out systems generated by the same evolutionary/skew-product process as training, which may overstate out-of-distribution generalization relative to truly novel dynamical systems.

Baselines focus on time-series foundation models; comparisons to specialized dynamical-systems models (e.g., reservoir computing, neural ODEs, SciML foundation models) or strong per-system baselines are missing.
Emergent PDE forecasting is demonstrated on only two PDEs (KS, VKVS), so the breadth of the claimed universality and PDE generalization remains somewhat limited.
Some interpretability claims (e.g., nonlinear resonance in attention) are compelling but qualitative and not causally tied to downstream forecast performance.
Reproducibility could be strengthened by releasing code, data, and trained checkpoints; the manuscript does not clearly state public availability.

strengths: Introduces a novel evolutionary framework for generating a large, diverse dataset of ~2e4 chaotic ODEs, enabling pretraining on rich dynamical structure rather than generic time series.

Proposes a principled architecture for chaotic dynamics, combining patched tokenization, temporal attention, channel attention, and dynamics-informed embeddings (random polynomial/Fourier features) motivated by Takens' theorem and Koopman/eDMD.

Demonstrates strong zero-shot forecasting on held-out chaotic ODEs, real experimental systems (double pendulum, C. elegans, electronic circuits), and two PDEs, outperforming competitive time series foundation models such as Chronos and TimesFM.

Provides an interesting scaling law showing that zero-shot performance improves with the number of unique dynamical systems in pretraining data while holding total timepoints constant, offering insight into data diversity for SciML foundation models.

Evaluation is extensive: multiple metrics (short-term error and long-term distributional/invariant statistics), statistical significance tests, ablations, and detailed appendices with completions, attention analysis, and additional baselines.
Addresses a timely and important problem in SciML: out-of-domain generalization and universal forecasting of chaotic dynamical systems.
Well-written and clearly structured, with strong visualizations and sufficient technical detail for expert readers.
weaknesses: The final model configuration and benefit of MLM pretraining are somewhat ambiguous: the paper reports that MLM improves some metrics but degrades autoregressive rollout, and it is not fully clear which configuration is used for all headline results.

The main ODE zero-shot test set is generated by the same evolutionary process as the training data, so it primarily tests generalization to unseen descendants of held-out founders rather than to arbitrary chaotic ODEs, limiting external validity of the core ODE claim.

PDE zero-shot forecasting is demonstrated on only two weakly turbulent PDE benchmarks with dimensionality reduction; broader claims about emergent PDE capability would benefit from more diverse and higher-dimensional PDE evaluations.

Reproducibility is not fully addressed: there is no explicit mention of code or dataset release, and some architecture/training choices (e.g., random feature dimensions, loss details) are relegated to appendices, which may hinder replication.

Baseline comparisons focus on time series foundation models; comparisons to specialized dynamical systems methods (e.g., reservoir computing, neural ODEs, SINDy, or dynamical systems foundation models) are limited.

Channel attention is trained with a fixed input channel dimension (C=3) and then applied to much higher-dimensional systems at test time; the empirical results are promising, but the mechanism enabling such extrapolation is not fully analyzed.
The claimed 'neural scaling law for differential equations' is primarily a data-diversity scaling result; model-size scaling is only explored in the appendix and is less central to the main claim.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging SciML problem: out-of-domain generalization and zero-shot forecasting for chaotic dynamical systems.
Introduces a large synthetically generated dataset of chaotic ODEs using evolutionary mutation/recombination and chaos filters, which could be a useful resource.
Proposes a dynamics-inspired architecture combining patching, channel attention, and polynomial/Fourier patch embeddings, with ablations of several components.
Provides extensive experiments across held-out synthetic systems, a few experimental datasets, two PDE benchmarks, distributional metrics, and a scaling-law analysis.
Reports statistical significance tests against several time-series foundation model baselines.
weaknesses: The central zero-shot generalization claim is mostly evaluated on synthetic systems generated by the same evolutionary/skew-product process as the training data, so it does not provide strong evidence of true out-of-domain generalization or real-world dynamical forecasting.

The baselines are insufficient for isolating the paper's contributions: there are no dynamics-specific multivariate baselines, no neural ODE/operator-learning/PDE foundation-model comparisons, and no strong multivariate time-series models trained on the same dataset.

The claimed emergent PDE forecasting ability is overclaimed: it is shown on only two reduced PDE benchmarks, against univariate time-series baselines, and the model is not compared to PDE-specific methods such as neural operators or PDE foundation models.

The model is trained by sampling only 3 channels per trajectory, yet inference claims multivariate generalization to arbitrary channel dimensions; this mismatch is not adequately validated and weakens the claimed channel-attention benefit.

The dataset may not represent truly novel or diverse chaotic dynamics: it is built from only 129 founder systems via a specific skew-product coupling, potentially limiting diversity and leaking dynamical motifs into the held-out test set.

Some evaluation and model-selection claims are selective: several invariant/geometric metrics in the appendix favor baselines, the MLM ablation degrades rollout performance, and the final model choice is not convincingly justified.

The scaling-law result is based on a small number of dataset splits and does not clearly establish a general neural scaling law for differential equations or separate system diversity from other confounds.
Reproducibility is limited: the paper does not provide code, model checkpoints, or the generated dataset, and the evolutionary search/integration pipeline is expensive and difficult to reproduce.
The paper relies on strong wording such as 'universal model', 'foundation model', and 'spontaneous PDE prediction', but the evidence does not support such broad conclusions.
Positioning relative to prior work is incomplete, especially for recent dynamics foundation models, PDE foundation models, and physics-informed/operator-learning baselines.

strengths: Introduces a novel, extensible synthetic dataset of ~20,000 chaotic ODEs generated through evolutionary mutation/recombination of known chaotic systems, with attractor-based selection and chaos validation.

Proposes a dynamics-informed architecture that combines patching, temporal and channel attention, and DMD-inspired polynomial/Fourier embeddings, with clear theoretical motivation from Takens' theorem and Koopman/eDMD ideas.

Provides extensive zero-shot evaluation on ~9,300 held-out chaotic systems across multiple short-term and long-term metrics, with statistically significant improvements over strong time-series baselines including Chronos and TimesFM.
Demonstrates generalization beyond training distribution: zero-shot forecasting of real experimental data and emergent PDE forecasting without retraining on PDE data.
Reports a scaling law for dynamical diversity while holding total training timepoints constant, offering a useful SciML insight distinct from standard data-scaling laws.

Includes informative ablations on channel attention, dynamics embeddings, MLM pretraining, and patch size, as well as substantial appendix material on data generation, metrics, attention analysis, and failure modes.
weaknesses: The emergent PDE forecasting claim is demonstrated only on two PDE benchmarks and mainly against generic time-series baselines; comparisons to specialized PDE foundation models or neural operators are missing.

The dataset generation process may induce structural biases due to its evolutionary starting point of 129 founder systems and skew-product recombination; although invariant distributions are analyzed, broad coverage of chaotic dynamics is not fully guaranteed.
Some evaluation details are inconsistent: TimeMoE yields NaNs, MLM helps completion but degrades autoregressive rollout, and the best training objective for forecasting remains unresolved.

Zero-shot experimental evaluation is promising but narrow, covering three datasets and mostly comparing against Chronos-SFT; adaptation/fine-tuning baselines and more real-world systems would strengthen external validity.
Long-horizon pointwise forecasts still show mean-regression, and the distributional metrics, while favorable, do not fully eliminate concerns about long-term attractor fidelity.

Reproducibility would benefit from explicit code/data release and more detailed documentation of the evolutionary discovery and filtering pipeline, even though the appendix provides substantial implementation details.

strengths: Introduces a novel and extensible evolutionary framework for generating a large dataset of chaotic ODEs, with careful chaos-preserving selection criteria and diversity analysis.

Proposes Panda, a dynamics-informed transformer architecture with patched tokenization, channel attention, and dynamic-mode-inspired embeddings, showing strong zero-shot forecasting on held-out chaotic systems.
Provides a comprehensive empirical evaluation across many held-out systems, metrics, prediction horizons, and baselines, including statistical significance tests and ablations.
Demonstrates zero-shot generalization to real-world experimental time series and emergent PDE forecasting, which are compelling and potentially high-impact results.
Reports a data-diversity neural scaling law for dynamical systems, offering a useful empirical finding for pretraining in SciML.
Includes interpretability analyses of attention maps and nonlinear resonance, adding insight beyond raw forecasting performance.
The paper is generally well-organized, clearly motivated, and positions itself well relative to prior work on time-series foundation models and dynamical systems.
weaknesses: The Chronos-SFT baseline is described as finetuned on 'our entire chaotic systems dataset', which is ambiguous; if it includes held-out systems, the comparison is invalid due to leakage and should be clarified.

The PDE comparison is not fully apples-to-apples: Panda is zero-shot while FNO/DeepONet are trained under different settings and limited to one-step prediction, so the claimed advantage requires more careful qualification.
The reproducibility statement in the extracted manuscript lacks concrete URLs or access details for code and model weights, making reproducibility harder to assess.

The role of MLM pretraining is somewhat inconsistent: it is listed as a key contribution but ablations show it can degrade autoregressive rollout, and the final forecast model configuration is not fully clear.
The train/test split for the evolutionary dataset could use stronger guarantees against lineage leakage beyond direct descendants, such as shared parent systems or sibling relationships.
The model is trained with fixed 3-channel inputs but evaluated on arbitrary-dimensional systems and PDEs; the mechanism for channel-count generalization is not fully explained or stress-tested.
The scaling law is empirical and only over dataset diversity for one architecture; it lacks theoretical grounding and broader compute/model-size scaling analysis.
Some interpretability claims, such as nonlinear resonance, are qualitative and would benefit from more rigorous quantitative validation.
Real-world experimental validation, while promising, covers only three datasets and does not deeply analyze robustness to noise, nonstationarity, or missing data.

strengths: Introduces a large synthetic dataset of chaotic ODEs generated via evolutionary recombination of 129 known systems, which could be a useful resource for SciML and dynamical systems research.
Ambitious zero-shot forecasting evaluation on a large held-out set of unseen synthetic chaotic systems, with comparisons to several time series foundation models.

Includes real-world experimental datasets (double pendulum, C. elegans, electronic circuits) and PDE benchmarks (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, von Karman vortex street), going beyond purely synthetic evaluation.
The architecture combines patched tokenization, channel attention, and dynamics-inspired embeddings (random Fourier/polynomial features), with ablations exploring their contributions.
Demonstrates a data-diversity scaling trend where zero-shot error decreases as the number of unique dynamical systems increases while total training timepoints are fixed.
Provides statistical significance tests, additional metrics in appendices, and a reproducibility statement with links to code/checkpoints.
Attention-based interpretability analyses attempt to connect model behavior to dynamical systems concepts such as resonance and recurrence.
The paper is generally well-organized and covers a broad range of experiments, from synthetic ODEs to real experimental time series and PDEs.
weaknesses: The central claim of zero-shot PDE forecasting is not convincingly supported. PDE inputs are preprocessed via Fourier modes or PCA into low-dimensional channels, and the operator-learning baselines (FNO, DeepONet) are trained in a limited one-step/context-window regime that is not directly comparable to Panda's long-context rollout. The reported PDE superiority may therefore be an artifact of unfair evaluation rather than genuine zero-shot PDE capability.

Training uses only 3-channel subsets of trajectories, yet the model is claimed to generalize to arbitrary-dimensional systems and high-dimensional PDEs. The model never sees more than 3 channels during training, creating a severe train/test mismatch. The mechanism by which channel attention extrapolates to 64 or 512 channels is not explained or validated, making the multivariate generalization claim questionable.

The dataset generation is less novel than claimed: it mainly applies parameter mutation and additive skew-product coupling to a fixed set of 129 known ODEs, followed by chaos filtering. This does not discover new functional forms beyond recombinations of existing systems, and the evolutionary search is relatively simple.

Real-world experimental evaluations are narrow, with essentially only Chronos-SFT as a baseline and no fair comparison to specialized multivariate dynamical systems models, reservoir computing methods, or the contemporaneous DynaMix under matched settings.

Long-term distributional metrics do not consistently favor Panda. For example, KL divergence becomes worse than Chronos-SFT at longer horizons, and the paper acknowledges mean regression. The abstract's claim of preserving distributional measures is therefore overstated.

Ablations show that MLM pretraining can reduce autoregressive rollout performance and interacts negatively with the dynamics embedding. The final architecture rationale is unclear, and it is not convincingly shown why MLM should be included for forecasting.

The interpretability analyses are largely qualitative and disconnected from performance. Attention entropy on sinusoids and attention map visualizations do not provide strong evidence for 'nonlinear resonance patterns' or a meaningful dynamical forecast strategy.

The 'neural scaling law for differential equations' is really a data-diversity scaling result: it shows that more unique systems help while total timepoints are fixed. This is interesting but not the same as a general neural scaling law for differential equations, and the power-law fit alone does not establish broad significance.

Baseline fairness is uneven. Chronos-SFT is fine-tuned on the full synthetic dataset, but other time series foundation models are used off-the-shelf, and PDE operator-learning baselines are not trained comparably. This makes headline comparisons potentially misleading.

Reproducibility is limited by the very expensive evolutionary data-generation pipeline, complex selection criteria, and large-scale integration. Exact thresholds, failure rates, and dataset coverage are not fully specified, making independent reproduction difficult.

The paper's broad claims—'emergent PDE forecasting,' 'global forecast model,' and 'interpretable internal representations'—are stronger than the evidence presented. A top-tier venue would require more rigorous validation of these central claims.

strengths: Introduces a novel, extensible synthetic dataset of ~20,000 chaotic ODEs discovered via evolutionary recombination of known chaotic systems, with attractor-based filtering and held-out founder controls.

Presents Panda, a pretrained patched transformer with channel attention and dynamics-inspired embeddings, showing strong zero-shot forecasting on unseen synthetic chaotic systems and competitive performance against time-series foundation models.
Demonstrates zero-shot transfer to real experimental data (double pendulum, C. elegans, electronic circuits), including an analysis of when channel attention helps as coupling strength increases.
Provides evidence of emergent zero-shot PDE forecasting on Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and von Karman vortex street benchmarks without PDE training data.
Includes a neural scaling law showing the importance of dynamical diversity versus repeated initial conditions, which is an interesting and domain-informed result.
Evaluation is extensive: 9.3k held-out systems, multiple metrics, statistical significance tests, ablations, long-horizon distributional metrics, and reproducibility resources (code and checkpoints).
Offers interpretability analyses of attention maps, including resonance-like frequency responses and structural patterns in temporal attention.
weaknesses: The synthetic test set is generated by the same evolutionary process as training and includes descendants of held-out systems, so it may overstate true out-of-domain generalization relative to completely novel dynamical systems.
Real-world validation is limited to three experimental datasets; broader validation on more diverse real chaotic systems would strengthen the central claims.

The architecture is largely an adaptation/combination of existing components (PatchTST, channel attention, random Fourier/polynomial features, MLM, p-RoPE); the main novelty lies in the dataset and application rather than a fundamentally new modeling mechanism.

PDE comparisons may be not fully apples-to-apples: FNO/DeepONet are trained for one-step prediction and rolled out, while Panda operates with much larger multivariate context and prediction horizons. The authors acknowledge this, but claims of outperforming fully trained PDE models should be interpreted cautiously.

Ablation results on MLM and dynamics embeddings are somewhat mixed: MLM helps forecasting but hurts autoregressive rollout, and its combination with the dynamics embedding can degrade performance, complicating the final architectural story.
Interpretability claims such as nonlinear resonance and attention-map structures are mostly qualitative and are not clearly tied to quantitative forecasting improvements.

The scaling law and emergent PDE forecasting are demonstrated on relatively low-dimensional or weakly turbulent systems, leaving open how well the approach extends to genuinely high-dimensional, strongly turbulent, or nonstationary real-world dynamics.
